story_pergunta: At your company, who checks what the AI agent is allowed to do?

slides.eyebrow: AI ON THE RISE · INTENT CONTRACTS
slides.headline: Safe agents don't need smarter planners. They need fewer tools.
slides.sub: A new paper takes every tool away from the planning model.

slides.headline: A paper strips the tools from the planner
slides.body: The planner submits a logged contract: a goal, a verbatim quote of the user, and scope fields. Code validates it. A small trusted model checks it against the user's words and writes the tool call itself.

slides.label: tasks completed with contracts vs 16/30 with a command reviewer
slides.sub: When the planner added work the user never asked for.

slides.headline: What I see in companies: agents act, and nobody can say why
items: The agent has broad tool access, and permission is an afterthought
There is no record of what the agent intended before it acted
A reviewer can only block the whole action, so teams switch it off

slides.headline: Multi-agent in production at an enterprise account
items: A multi-agent platform running in production at a US$5.5 million account
Multi-agent in production requires an audited defect log

slides.headline: Simple that works beats complex that impresses.
slides.body: The paper is honest: contracts did not reduce unauthorized actions versus blind review. They add a complete pre-action record and let the trusted side do only the authorized part. In practice, a hard permission layer in plain code beats a smarter planner.

slides.eyebrow: WANT TO SEE HOW I DID IT?
slides.headline: Comment AGENTS.
slides.body: I'll send you the step-by-step of this case by DM. I take AI off the drawing board and put it into production, with measured results.

caption:
A new paper on Hugging Face Papers takes every tool away from the planning model. The planner only states its intent: a goal, a verbatim quote of the user, and scope fields. Code validates the contract. A small trusted model writes the tool call.

The result worth reading: when the planner added work the user never asked for, contracts completed the user's task in 27 of 30 runs. A reviewer that sees the intent completed 16 of 30, because it can only refuse a whole command.

The authors also report that contracts did not reduce unauthorized actions compared with a blind reviewer. One model pair, benign over-reach only. I respect that candor.

What I see in companies: agents get broad access, nobody records intent before the action, and review becomes all-or-nothing.

I run a multi-agent platform in production at a US$5.5 million account. About 60% efficiency gain, and multi-agent in production requires an audited defect log. My view: reliability comes from a hard permission layer, not a smarter planner. The model proposes. Plain code decides.

Comment AGENTS and I'll DM you how I did it.

Sources: huggingface.co
